A feedstock evaluation quantified available resources at a defined radius for each of the 10 airports selected by Massport. A TEA was conducted to estimate the volumes of renewable fuel and SAF production and comparative production costs for feedstocks and their associated production pathways. ORH and BAF were selected as the primary locations for the TEA due to its proximity to feedstocks, infrastructure, and locations outside of Boston, where space is less of an issue compared with dense urban environments. PWM was selected for the woody biomass TEA due to Maine’s prevalent wood industry. Generally, biofuels plants are most economical when they are located near abundant feedstocks. There are multiple potential feedstocks and technology pathways. As production grows, certain feedstocks and pathways may provide economic advantages. 2.1 Feedstock Evaluation An evaluation was conducted to identify the feedstocks suitable for SAF production and their associated volumes for each of the 10 airports selected for this study (Figure 5). It is important to note that due to the proximity of these airports to one another, the radii overlap. While this evaluation is focused on SAF production, these feedstocks could also be considered for other bioenergy production. Figure 5. The following resources are considered in this study: • Vegetable oils and byproducts include soybean oil and distillers corn oil (DCO), a byproduct of ethanol production. Other vegetable oils in the United States include canola, corn, cottonseed, sunflower, and safflower, but these are produced at a much smaller quantity and are used primarily in food-grade applications. Annual crops such as camelina and pennycress have received attention in recent years, but their commercial production is still under development. Data on soybean crushing facilities was obtained from the National Oilseed Processors Association (NOPA, 2024). To evaluate the availability of DCO, we considered existing ethanol production plants in the region obtained from the Ethanol Producer Magazine (2024). • FOG includes animal fats (e.g., tallow, white grease, and poultry fat) obtained from slaughterhouse and livestock farm waste, yellow grease (rendered used cooking oil generated at commercial and industrial cooking operations), and brown grease (rendered trap/interceptor grease recovered from traps installed in the sewage lines of restaurants/food processing plants and wastewater treatment plants) (Milbrandt et al. 2018).
